## Part I — Application Links & System Architecture

- **Interactive Shiny App URL:** <https://jordanblackman.shinyapps.io/ads506-retail-forecasting-app/>
- **Source Code Repository:** <https://github.com/jblackman-bit/ADS-506/tree/main/Module%205>

**App Description:** This Shiny app provides an interactive forecasting platform analyzing 416 months (1992–2026) of U.S. Census Bureau retail trade sales. Designed for people working in supply chain analysis, the application displays real purchasing volume (CPI-adjusted) and nominal retail sales, dynamically fits predictive algorithms (TSLM, ETS, Seasonal ARIMA, Ensemble Combo), and separates validation backtesting from forecasting future periods.

**Core Application Features:**

- **Dynamic Data Exploration:** Interactive vertical filtering, historical date range controls, and real (CPI-deflated) vs. nominal valuation toggle to isolate true consumer demand from monetary inflation.
- **Decoupled Analytical Engine:** Separates historical validation backtesting (Model & Accuracy tab) from 6- to 36-month forward production forecasts (Comparative Forecasts tab). Forecast data can be downloaded as a CSV on the Comparative Forecasts tab.
- **Executive Diagnostics & Intervals:** Color-coded out-of-sample and in-sample accuracy metrics in one table and 80%/95% prediction intervals with actual historic data.

## Part II — Executive Data Story

**Context: Structural Divergence Behind Macro Aggregates**\
Aggregated retail totals hide important patterns across various consumer sectors. While essential Health & Personal Care exhibits consistent growth (+180% since 1992), discretionary Clothing & Accessories volume has remained completely flat for 24 years with massive December holiday surges. Building materials peaks in May--June aligned with macroeconomic cycles. Reliable supply chain planning requires models that accommodate these contrasting seasonal and cyclical dynamics.

### Strategic Conflict: Why Does Linear Regression (TSLM) Fail?

When evaluating out-of-sample forecast accuracy over a 12-month validation horizon, **Time Series Linear Models (TSLM)** perform drastically worse than the other algorithms across every retail vertical, generating **2.1**$\times$ to 4.6$\times$ higher forecast errors (e.g., RMSE of \$9,108M for TSLM vs. \$1,975M for ETS). This severe failure occurs because of three fundamental limitations:

1.  **Rigid Deterministic Trend:** By default, TSLM enforces a static, straight-line slope ($\beta_1 t$). It cannot adapt to structural economic inflections, recessions (2001, 2008, 2020), or compounding curves (Health exponential expansion vs. Apparel stagnation), leading to massive multi-billion-dollar baseline drift.
2.  **Static Additive Seasonality:** TSLM fits constant seasonal dummy coefficients ($\sum \gamma_j D_j$), forcing identical dollar swings each year. Because real retail demand is *multiplicative*, holiday surges expand in dollar scale as total revenue grows; TSLM severely underestimates Q4 peaks and distorts troughs.
3.  **Zero Dynamic Memory (White Noise Error Assumption):** Ordinary least squares assumes independent errors, ignoring serial correlation and multi-month supply shocks. Unlike ARIMA and ETS, TSLM cannot self-correct after an initial forecast error.

**Remedying TSLM Issues in Practice:**\
To salvage TSLM for retail operations, planners must: (a) employ **Dynamic Regression (ARMAX)** incorporating macroeconomic regressors such as **CPI (inflation deflator)**, disposable income, and consumer sentiment into the error structure; (b) incorporate **calendar/trading-day regressors** (counting peak shopping Saturdays and days between Thanksgiving and Christmas); and (c) apply **logarithmic transformations** ($\log Y_t$) or spline trends to model multiplicative seasonal growth and cyclical bending.

\vspace{-4pt}

**Resolution & Implementation:** Operational planners must abandon rigid OLS models for inventory commitments. Supply chains should deploy $\text{ETS}(M,A,M)$ for apparel holiday planning and Seasonal ARIMA for housing materials, preventing costly stockouts while maintaining lean working capital.\
